newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tax changes may not change Japan liquor habits.
newsitem.headline: Tax changes may not change Japan liquor habits.

text.p: A major overhaul of Japan's liquor tax system should boost sales of imported whiskey, but the changes may not be enough to pull Japanese consumers away from their favourite domestic drinks, analysts say.

The government will start cutting duties on imported whiskey and spirits and will raise taxes on such domestic liquor as the highly potent shochu from this October after losing a World Trade Organisation (WTO) ruling last year.
"The number of shochu drinkers may fall because of the price hike, but will they all drift to whiskey? They may shift to beer or wine," said an industry analyst at a Japanese securities firm.
Industry sources said that beer accounts for more than 50 percent of all alcoholic drinks consumed in Japan, while shochu accounts for about 30 percent and whiskey around 10 percent.

So-called brown spirits -- including French cognac and Scotch whisky, are currently taxed up to six times more heavily than the domestic product while white spirits -- vodka and gin -- are taxed 2.4 times higher.

Shochu -- a potent, colourless liquor -- costs about 1,240 yen to 1,350 yen ($10 to $11) per 1.8 litre. With the initial increase in liquor tax slated for October, plus a hike in Japan's consumption tax in April, the price of shochu will rise by 100 yen ($826) later this year and will end up around 1,440 yen to 1,630 yen ($11 to $13) by October 1998, industry sources said.
The current average price of imported whiskey is about 3,000 yen to 4,000 yen ($24 to $33) per 0.7 litre, which will likely be reduced about by about 400 yen to 500 yen ($3 to $4), they said.
Some consumers said the prices changes are not enough to make them change their habits.

"I don't drink either whiskey or shochu. I'll keep on drinking beer. I also choose drinks according to what I eat. If it's Western-style dinner, I drink wine," said Shogo Kawamura, a 29-year-old computer programmer.
"I'll keep drinking shochu even if the tax goes up. I drink shochu because I like it, not because it's cheap," said Mitsuro Shimizu, a book editor in his mid-40s.
But if there was any shift towards whiskey, imports would benefit more than domestically produced brands, said Tokushi Yamasaki, an analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research Ltd.

The Scotch Whisky Association of Britain told Reuters that it was organising a trade mission to Osaka and Tokyo in mid-April, together with Britain's Department of Trade and Industry to help British companies prepare for the tax reforms.

"The removal of the tax discrimination will allow Scotch whisky to compete much better. The British government recently suggested that the removal of the tax discrimination would boost sales of Scotch by as much as 75 million pounds ($122 million)," it said.

"We'll be affected by the liquor tax changes. It's very difficult to access changes in consumer preferences, but we hope the damage will be limited," said a spokesman for major Japanese shochu maker Takara Shuzo Co Ltd.
The WTO ruling was the result of complaints by the European Union, the United States and Canada that Japan taxes foreign spirits at levels higher than for domestic liquor. ($1=121 yen)
